OpenAI launches Health in ChatGPT

Health is a new mode in which the chatbot gains access to your medical records and Apple Watch data to answer health-related questions based on your actual metrics.

Users can connect Apple Health along with medical records from hospital systems, One Medical, or Function Health. Once linked, ChatGPT can view lab results, medications, recent doctor visits, sleep, and activity data. It can compare a new blood test with previous ones, explain unclear terms from discharge summaries, or even recommend restaurants while taking allergies into account.

According to OpenAI’s own statistics, 300 million people already ask ChatGPT about health every week. Among early testers, 70% of these conversations began outside a dedicated medical section. For this reason, the relevant context is now pulled directly into regular chats without the need to switch modes.

Dedicated models have been assigned to the feature. Free users get access to GPT-5.5 Instant, which has improved recognition of situations that require a real doctor. Paid users receive GPT-5.6 Sol, which handles complex cases more accurately and explains lab results more effectively.
Data from medical records and Apple Health is not used for model training or advertising targeting. It is stored with additional encryption, can be disconnected at any time, and synchronized records are deleted within 30 days.

The feature is currently available only in the United States, on web and iOS, for users aged 18 and older on the Free, Go, Plus, and Pro plans. It is not available in Codex.

U-Net by hand ✍️ ~ 17 steps walkthrough below

I consider U-Net as a key milestone in deep learning, the first image-to-image model that really worked!

It came out of medical imaging, an unusual place, not from NeurIPS or CVPR or ACL.

Now it is the backbone of diffusion models, which you see in almost all modern image generation models.

I drew the network as a C so the matrix multiplication flows naturally down.

Tilt your head to the right and it is a U again. 🤣

Goal: push a 3 x 16 image down to a 2 x 4 bottleneck and back out again, filling in every cell yourself.

= 1. Given =

An image of three channels, R, G and B, sixteen pixels wide, and every kernel the network will use.

= 2. Convolution 1 =

Let us slide the first kernel over the image. Each output is one multiply-and-add over a 2 x 3 window, and the result is the green feature map.

= 3. Find the maxima =

We circle the largest value in each 1 x 2 window. Circling first is worth the extra step: it is the pooling decision, made before anything is written down.

= 4. Max pool 1 =

Let us copy those maxima down. Sixteen columns become eight, and half the detail is gone for good.

= 5. Convolution 2 =

We convolve again with the second kernel, deeper into the contracting path. The feature map is blue now.

= 6. Find the maxima again =

Same move as step 3, on the blue map.

= 7. Max pool 2 =

Eight columns become four.

= 8. The bottleneck =

Let us convolve once more. This is the bottom of the U, a 2 x 4 block that is everything the network kept.

= 9. Spread it out =

We start back up. The transposed convolution writes each bottleneck value into a wider grid, leaving gaps between them.

= 10. Transposed convolution 1 =

Let us fill those gaps by convolving over the spread-out grid. Four columns become eight.

= 11. The first skip =

We copy the encoder's matching row straight across. This is the skip connection, and it is the whole reason a U-Net can recover detail that pooling threw away.

= 12. Convolution with the skip =

Let us convolve the upsampled features together with the copied ones.

= 13. Spread it out again =

Same as step 9, one level up.

= 14. Transposed convolution 2 =

Eight columns become sixteen, back to the width we started at.

= 15. The second skip =

The encoder's first feature map comes across, the one made before any pooling happened.

= 16. Convolution and ReLU =

We convolve, then cross out every negative and set it to zero.

= 17. Output convolution =

Let us apply the last kernel. Out comes R', G' and B', an image the same size as the one we started with.

The outputs:

R' = [3, 0, 7, 0, 7, 0, 17, 0, 3, 0, 9, 0, 2, 0, 6, 0]
G' = [1, 20, 1, 10, 1, 12, 1, 19, 2, 5, 1, 11, 1, 3, 1, 7]
B' = [4, 20, 8, 10, 8, 12, 18, 19, 5, 5, 10, 11, 3, 3, 7, 7]
Congrats! You just calculated a U-Net by hand.

Gadi Eisenkot wants Israelis to enjoy their beach vacation in Cyprus. His billboards near Larnaca airport say so directly: "Israelis, enjoy! You deserve it," followed by a second sign on the way home: "Landed? Had fun? Now come back and win!"

A Cypriot MEP is now demanding a ban on foreign election ads, which means Eisenkot has achieved something Netanyahu never managed: uniting Cypriots against Israeli politics.

Back home, the general-turned-candidate has bigger enemies than tourism regulators — namely, his own bloc. 

"A reality where a party leader with 8 to 10 seats demands the premiership is not appropriate," Eisenkot said, a line he's repeated for months, most recently aimed squarely at Naftali Bennett. 

Translation from campaign-speak: I have more mandates in the polls, so kindly step aside and let the man with the bigger poll number run the country.

Meanwhile, Yashar! just recruited Eliana Sachs, 25, model and social activist from Beer Sheva, who lost her mother and brother to an Iranian missile strike on the city, to run the party's youth wing. 

Eisenkot called her "the Israel of today — determined, values-driven, a true blend of action and spirit". Grief, rebranded as campaign strategy, is apparently the fastest-growing sector in Israeli politics this cycle.

And when Ynet's Moran Azoulai pressed him on his own record, Eisenkot didn't dodge — he doubled down: "As chief of staff I said that until the bodies of the fallen are returned, I won't approve bringing in workers from Gaza. 
Not one laborer entered from Gaza in all four years I served as chief of staff." A hard line delivered with the confidence of a man who knows exactly how many mandates that kind of sentence is worth in October.

So who's actually running this campaign — the candidate polling ahead of Netanyahu, or the grief, the guilt, and the billboards doing the polling for him?
